prize_parts.citation: for the invention of the optical lattice clock based on magic-wavelength trapping and its realisation at the 10^-18 level of fractional uncertainty

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single part, optical lattice clocks, credited to Katori and Ye. After the first round I can answer the chair's distinctness question more concretely than I did before. The comb (2005) made optical frequencies countable, and ion control (2012) showed how to interrogate one quantum system with great care. Neither solves the problem the lattice clock solves, which is to hold thousands of neutral atoms at once with Doppler and recoil shifts removed and the light shift cancelled by the choice of wavelength, so that statistical averaging and accuracy improve together. That is a different physical mechanism and a different instrument, and the evidence is in the numbers: independent labs (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE and others) now compare lattice clocks at the 1e-18 level, resolve gravitational redshift over millimetres and set limits on drifts of constants. Eight members have positions on this candidate and none has questioned the physics. I also take Mehlig's request to apply one bar to every candidate, and by that bar (mechanism identified, result reproduced, interpretation stable) the clock case is among the best on the list. The citation I propose rests on the lattice clock itself and deliberately says nothing about the comb or about optical clocks in general.
statement.case_against: The real weakness is still the boundary with 2005 and 2012, and I do not think it vanishes by drafting alone: a sceptical reader can say the lattice clock is the best use of the comb and of laser-cooling toolkits already honoured. I think the answer is that the magic-wavelength condition is a new idea rather than a use of an old one, but this is a judgement the committee must make explicitly. Second, the Katori and Ye split needs a primary-record check; Olsson is right that the proposal and the first strontium demonstrations are Katori's, whereas Ye's decisive contribution is the accuracy frontier, coherence and many-body clock physics, and a citation that says only 'invention' would under-describe Ye. Third, Lemonde, Gill, Bloom, Ludlow and Takamoto made real contributions; I judge that they do not displace either of the two named, but I cannot prove that from memory and would welcome an outside check. Finally, the redefinition of the second has not occurred, and the geodesy and dark-matter payoffs are still mostly prospective. I regard this as weaker than the other objections, since the capability is demonstrated, but it is not nothing.

responses.point: Olsson asks that the Katori and Ye boundary be checked against the 2003 to 2006 record, wording the citation as invention and development, and asks whether two parts could be considered, for example a method prize such as aberration-corrected microscopy beside B059.
responses.response: I agree with the wording point and have changed my citation accordingly: it now says invention (Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and first strontium demonstrations) and realisation at the 10^-18 level (the Ye line), so that the two names carry two separable contributions. On a second part I would not support one this year. B027 is a legitimate method candidate, but you have recused yourself from it and noted that Krivanek is outside the credited names, and a two-part prize would need two clean attributions within the three-person cap. B059 already uses two names, which leaves one slot, and I do not think the committee should fill it merely because it is free. I would rather leave B027 for a year when it can be debated by the full committee.

responses.point: Lindroth argues that Lemonde, Gill and Bloom are not a reason for a third name because the concept and the record-setting realisation are well separated, and that Ye's comb work belongs to his career rather than to the cited achievement.
responses.response: I largely accept this and it moves me from doubt towards a working conclusion: Katori's concept and Ye's pushing of the clock to 1e-18 are what the field credits, and the other groups' contributions (SYRTE, NPL, NIST in the early lattice-clock demonstrations) were real but followed or paralleled rather than defined these two steps. I keep one reservation that I would like recorded: as an experimentalist I cannot fully verify the 2003 to 2006 chronology from memory, so I would still ask that a short priority check be done before the vote, and if it showed that another group demonstrated the cancellation of the light shift independently and earlier, I would revisit the pair. You are right that the citation must leave out the comb; I have kept it out.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks the Higgs discovery (B019) first as the largest unrecognised discovery and calls the attribution problem one of drafting, but concedes it omits Della Negra and says he is less convinced than before that the overlap objection to the lattice clock is strong.
responses.response: I accept the scale argument for the Higgs; as a physicist I would not dispute that finding that particle is bigger than a better clock. But I cannot agree that the attribution problem is only drafting. Two independent detectors, thousands of authors and a three-name cap mean that any trio reflects leadership roles at particular moments, and you name three people whilst conceding a fourth with a plausible claim. A prize that the physics community reads as arbitrary damages the discovery it honours. I also note that your own scientific payoff argument against the clock, that it is largely prospective, sits oddly with the fact that the clock has already delivered a millimetre-scale redshift measurement and 1e-18 comparisons that no other instrument gives. I am glad that you have moved on the overlap point.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, keeps IceCube (B043) first for new-window instrumentation, and in round 1 conceded that Halzen, Karle and Spiering is a defensible but compact allocation that leaves out the Baikal, AMANDA and DUMAND leaders.
responses.response: I share your preference for instruments that open a new window, and I regard the diffuse flux as secure. My difficulty is the one you recorded yourself: nobody in this room has settled who was decisive among Halzen, Karle, Spiering and the earlier pioneers, and for TXS 0506+056 and NGC 1068 the source-level evidence is still at a modest level of significance with KM3NeT confirmation still to come. The clock is the reverse case in both respects. If the committee could establish the decisive roles in the 2013 evidence and the 2017-2018 source associations, I would reconsider IceCube for a coming year, and I would count it above squeezed light, but I cannot move it above B059 on the present record.

responses.point: Johansson moved his first choice from circuit QED to B059, but asked whether Ye's credit is best attributed to the clock itself or partly to the comb work already honoured, and flagged his own possible recusal on B013.
responses.response: My answer is the one I gave Lindroth: Ye's credit in this configuration is for the strontium lattice clock, its stability and accuracy, and the many-body regime that he opened, which is separate from his work on comb stabilisation and ultrastable cavities; I would want the citation to state that. I respect your decision to treat circuit QED with caution given your own field, and I agree that it is distinct from the 2025 macroscopic tunnelling prize in what it demonstrates, though I think the committee would need to explain that distinction carefully and resolve Girvin's and Devoret's position. I keep B013 as my first alternative, and the reason is its scientific quality, not support counts.

responses.point: Mehlig asks that the same bar be applied consistently across the shortlist, notes that independent confirmation is the property he credits to topological insulators, and argues the 2016 prize does not cover the Z2 topological insulator.
responses.response: That is a fair challenge and I have tried to apply it. On your criterion, B016 is strong: the mechanism is identified, the 2007 HgTe measurement could have failed, and the interpretation has been stable for years. I do not have the expertise to judge your reading of the 2016 prize, so I defer to you and Eriksson on distinctness, and I accept that the redefinition of the second is a metrological milestone rather than an additional piece of understanding. My remaining reasons for placing B059 first are the cleaner attribution (Kane and Mele are joined by Molenkamp, with Hasan and Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang left out, which is a harder choice than Katori and Ye) and a distinct, quantitative payoff in measurement. If the committee decides not to proceed with B059, B016 would be a serious option for me.

uncertainties: Whether the 2003 to 2006 primary record supports Katori for the concept and first demonstrations and Ye for the accuracy frontier, with no earlier independent demonstration by Lemonde, Gill, Bloom or others; I recommend a short priority check by outside reviewers if the committee agrees.
Whether the committee accepts the magic-wavelength lattice clock as distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, which is a judgement of scientific substance rather than of wording.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second should be read as maturity or a reason to wait; I lean to maturity because the performance is already demonstrated.
My lack of expertise in condensed matter (B034, B016) and in collaboration attribution at ATLAS, CMS and IceCube makes my judgement on those candidates weaker than on B059.
statement.conflict_note: I spent a year in John Hall's laboratory during my PhD, and Hall's JILA group is the lineage in which Jun Ye worked, so there is a mentor-lineage connection to one proposed laureate, though I have no direct collaboration with Ye or Katori that I know of; I regard this as a distant scientific link rather than a conflict that requires recusal, and I leave the decision to the committee. I lead quantum-sensing work in WACQT, a Chalmers-led centre that overlaps institutionally with Johansson's home institution, which bears on B013 and not on B059. I have no other known conflicts for any shortlisted candidate.
